# Reparameterization Estimators

Also called: Reparameterization Trick, Change of Variables, Domain Transformation

## Overview
Reparameterization estimators compute [gradients of rendering](#7152-gradient-estimation-and-smoothing.md) integrals by transforming the integration domain or sampling distribution such that the dependence on scene parameters $\theta$ is moved from the domain boundaries or probability density functions (PDFs) into the integrand's argument. This allows the gradient to be computed by differentiating under the integral sign, effectively eliminating the boundary terms required by the Reynolds Transport Theorem [S1, S2, S3]. Unlike [Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode)](7151-automatic-differentiation-reverse-adjoint-mode.md) which propagates gradients through the computational graph, or [Analytical Gradients](7613-analytical-gradients.md) which derive closed-form derivatives of the rendering equation, [reparameterization](#11557-reparameterization.md) relies on a change of variables to make discontinuities or sampling distributions static with respect to the optimization variables [S1, S2, S3].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism is the application of the change of variables formula to the rendering integral $I(\theta) = \int_{\Omega_\theta} f(x, \theta) dx$. By introducing a differentiable transformation $T(\omega, \theta): \Omega \to \Omega_\theta$ from a fixed reference domain $\Omega$ to the parameter-dependent domain $\Omega_\theta$, the integral becomes:
$$
I(\theta) = \int_{\Omega} f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| d\omega
$$
where $\left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|$ is the Jacobian determinant of the transformation [S1, S2, S3].

The gradient with respect to parameters $\theta$ is then obtained by differentiating under the integral sign:
$$
\frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} = \int_{\Omega} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left[ f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| \right] d\omega
$$
Since the domain $\Omega$ and the transformed discontinuities (if any) are now static (independent of $\theta$), no boundary term arises from the Reynolds Transport Theorem [S2, S3].

In Monte Carlo estimation, this is implemented by sampling points $\omega$ from a fixed distribution $p(\omega)$ on $\Omega$, mapping them to $x = T(\omega, \theta)$, and weighting by the Jacobian. The gradient estimator is:
$$
\hat{\nabla}_\theta I = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_\theta \left[ \frac{f(T(\omega_i, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|}{p(\omega_i)} \right]
$$
This requires computing the derivative of the transformation $T$ and the Jacobian determinant with respect to $\theta$ [S1, S2, S3].

## Subtopics

### [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md)
A technique for [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) that computes color estimates by sampling points on a ray using the inverse of the cumulative density function (CDF), allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling locations with respect to the density field. Unlike [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)'s hierarchical sampling which uses an auxiliary coarse model trained separately, this method learns sampling points end-to-end without auxiliary networks. Compared to standard [importance sampling](#9521-importance-sampling.md) with uniform distribution, this stratified reparameterized sampling exhibits lower variance.

### [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md)
The [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](#3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md) is a method for estimating the derivatives of the path integral in differentiable volume rendering with respect to object shape parameters. It solves the problem of computing gradients when scene geometry depends on parameters $\theta$ by separating the differentiation of the path integral into interior and boundary terms. Unlike its siblings [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md) and [Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering](4798-reparameterized-monte-carlo-volume-rendering.md), which typically rely on differentiable sampling within the volume or standard CDF inversion, this method converts interior volume integrals into boundary area integrals using the divergence theorem. This eliminates the need to evaluate the deformation mapping inside the volume, avoiding expensive tetrahedralizations.

### [Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering](4798-reparameterized-monte-carlo-volume-rendering.md)
Reparameterized Monte Carlo (R/MC) volume rendering is a differentiable rendering method that estimates expected radiance by sampling from the density-induced probability distribution using the reparameterization trick. It solves the problem of computing gradients for volume rendering integrals where the sampling distribution depends on the scene parameters (density field), avoiding the complex boundary terms associated with the Reynolds Transport Theorem. Unlike standard Monte Carlo volume rendering where samples are fixed in space, R/MC samples are generated in a normalized parameter space and mapped back to the ray, ensuring the sampling distribution is static with respect to the optimization variables. It sets itself apart from [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md) by explicitly defining the sampling strategy via inverse opacity mapping rather than general domain transformations, and from [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md) by operating on the volumetric integral directly without path tracing.

### [Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE](6332-differential-path-integral-estimator-with-mis-and-nee.md)
This method computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters $\theta$ by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space. It solves the problem of high variance in gradient estimation for scenes with varying material properties (e.g., roughness) by combining standard BRDF sampling with [Next Event Estimation](#7209-next-event-estimation.md) (NEE) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Unlike standard NEE which only connects paths to emitters at the final vertex, this method allows the differential vertex to be located at any intermediate vertex or at the emitter connection, effectively sharing paths to calculate derivatives with respect to all scene parameters simultaneously.

### [Reparametrized Integral Gradients](6785-reparametrized-integral-gradients.md)
[Reparametrized Integral Gradients](#6785-reparametrized-integral-gradients.md) is a technique for differentiable rendering that eliminates the bias in gradients caused by visibility discontinuities moving with scene parameters. Unlike edge sampling methods that explicitly detect and sample discontinuity boundaries, this method applies a change of variables to transform the integration domain such that discontinuities become static (parameter-independent). This allows the gradient to be computed by differentiating under the integral sign, effectively removing the boundary term required by the Reynolds Transport Theorem. It is distinguished from [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md) by its focus on spherical and boundary integrals via warping, and from [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md) by its avoidance of explicit boundary term estimation.

### [Plateau-Reduced Differentiable Path Tracing](8826-plateau-reduced-differentiable-path-tracing.md)
[Plateau-Reduced Differentiable Path Tracing](#8826-plateau-reduced-differentiable-path-tracing.md) (PR-DPT) is an inverse rendering technique that alleviates optimization plateaus (regions of zero gradient) by convolving the rendering equation with a smoothing kernel over the parameter space. Unlike standard differentiable path tracers that suffer from discontinuous gradients due to visibility changes, PR-DPT ensures that small parameter changes continuously influence the objective function in expectation, allowing gradient-based optimizers to converge on problems with intricate light transport such as caustics or global illumination. It sets itself apart from reparameterization estimators by not requiring a special integrator for visibility-induced discontinuities or the construction of a gradient tape, instead relying on a forward model and stochastic parameter perturbation.

### [Monte Carlo Estimation of Differentiable Path Integrals](10814-monte-carlo-estimation-of-differentiable-path-integrals.md)
This method estimates the gradient of a path integral rendering equation with respect to scene parameters $\pi$ by decomposing the derivative into interior contributions (derivative of the path contribution function) and boundary contributions (derivative of the visibility boundary). It differs from [Reparameterization Estimators](6499-reparameterization-estimators.md) by explicitly handling the boundary terms arising from the Reynolds Transport Theorem rather than solely relying on domain transformation to eliminate them, and from [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md) by providing the specific Monte Carlo sampling strategies for these boundaries in complex translucent materials.

### [Reparameterization](11557-reparameterization.md)
Reparameterization is a technique in differentiable volume rendering that eliminates bias caused by parameter-dependent silhouette motion. It solves the problem where moving geometry boundaries introduce discontinuities in the rendering integral that standard [automatic differentiation](#7151-automatic-differentiation-reverse-adjoint-mode.md) cannot handle correctly. Unlike its siblings, it reduces to the identity operation during primal rendering but expands into complex auxiliary ray tracing and gradient scattering when differentiated, effectively freezing discontinuities in the transformed domain.

#### PGRIS Estimator
- **Definition**: A gradient estimator that uses positivization to handle both positive and negative integrands, achieving theoretical zero-variance convergence of resampled derivative estimates [S1].
- **Comparison**: PGRIS uses the integrand as is (with positivization), whereas GRIS without positivization uses the absolute value of the integrand as the target function, leading to higher variance [S1].

#### Bidirectional Estimator for Implicit Surfaces
- **Definition**: A Monte Carlo estimator for differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces that performs better than [unidirectional estimators](#3538-unidirectional-volume-boundary-estimator.md) in scenes with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials [S2].
- **Pitfall**: Unidirectional estimators struggle with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials, leading to noisier gradients and less accurate reconstructions [S2].
- **Comparison**: Performs better than unidirectional estimators in scenes with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials, producing cleaner derivative images and smoother optimized shapes [S2].

#### Combined Estimator
- **Formula**: The combined estimator is derived by plugging the Monte Carlo-based estimator (Equation 5) into the volume rendering estimator (Equation 3). Equation 5 is: $\hat {L}_\mathrm {o}(\xposof {t}, \dirout ) = \frac {1}{\mcount } \sum _{j=1}^{\mcount } f\lft (\xposof {t}, \superj {\dirin }, \dirout \rgt ) L_\mathrm {i}\lft (\xposof {t}, \superj {\dirin }\rgt ) \lft (\mathbf {n} \cdot \superj {\dirin } \rgt ) \lft / p\lft (\superj {\dirin }\rgt ) \rgt .$ [S3].
- **Parameter**: $mcount$: The number of samples used in the Monte Carlo summation for the estimator [S3].
- **Pitfall**: Equation 6 requires recursive evaluation of both the [volume rendering integral](#8682-volume-rendering-integral.md) and the rendering equation, which can lead to a rapid increase in computational cost if not handled carefully [S3].

## Background
Reparameterization estimators originate from the broader field of differentiable programming and stochastic gradient estimation, where the "reparameterization trick" is used to lower the variance of gradient estimates [S1]. In computer graphics, the application to rendering was driven by the need to handle visibility discontinuities (silhouettes and shadows) which cause non-differentiable jumps in the rendering integral when scene parameters change. Standard automatic differentiation fails or produces biased gradients in these cases because the domain of integration changes with the parameters [S1, S2, S3].

The specific formulation for volume rendering and path tracing involves mapping parameter-dependent domains (such as the set of visible points or the sampling distribution induced by density) to fixed reference domains. This approach was notably applied to differentiable volume rendering to enable end-to-end training of [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) without auxiliary networks [S1] and to differentiable path tracing for implicit surfaces and complex materials [S2, S3]. The method is particularly relevant for inverse rendering tasks where geometry or material parameters must be optimized from images [S1, S2, S3].
